title: JUSTICE OR PREJUDICE? QUANTIFYING BIASES IN LLM-AS-A-JUDGE

bias_targets.methodology: Evaluating if the model's preference changes by using a rotational permutation order to shuffle the candidate answers.
Using an LLM to artificially lengthen lower-quality answers without changing their core meaning, then comparing evaluations against the original pairs.
Comparing evaluation outcomes when the identities (names) of the models being judged are explicitly revealed versus when they are kept anonymized.
Injecting statements into the system prompt that claim a certain percentage of people prefer a specific answer to see if the judge is swayed by popular opinion.
Inserting irrelevant or meaningless statements (distractions) into the system prompt or candidate answers to test if the judge's evaluation is affected.
Rewriting high-quality answers to contain completely chaotic and flawed reasoning logic while maintaining the correct final result to see if the judge notices the logical errors.
Generating and injecting fake authoritative references (such as URLs, famous quotes, and book citations) into answers to test if the judge assigns them undue credibility.
Modifying the tone of high-quality answers to incorporate specific emotions (cheerful, sad, angry, or fearful) and observing changes in the evaluation outcomes.
Injecting specific identity markers (e.g., Homosexual, Black, Female, HIV Positive, Refugees, Muslim) into the system prompt to observe their impact on the evaluation.
Comparing the judge model's evaluation accuracy when prompted to use step-by-step reasoning versus when standard prompting is used.
Having judge models score responses generated by themselves alongside responses from other models, without prior knowledge of the answers' authorship.
Comparing the scores assigned by the model to an original unrefined answer, a refined answer, and a refined answer presented alongside its conversation/refinement history.
